title: Variation in wing dimensions in Mimon bennetti (Chiroptera: Phyllostomidae) are habitat and sex related
content:
Abstract
Related topics such as secondary sexual dimorphism, allometry and selection remain the subject of broad debates, requiring methodological adjustments, including greater data integration in analyses and reduction of sampling deficits. This is, in part, because these issues should be analysed at a level lower than the lineage. The southern golden bat Mimon bennettii (Phyllostomidae) is an excellent model for studying morphological variation, because previous data indicate that wing dimensions vary between sexes and environmental structures. In this context, we conducted a study involving 11 skeletal components of the wing, with a total of 14 variables relating them to skull size as proxy of body size, and we used an available molecular phylogeny as a basis for some inferences about wing morphology. The results corroborate the hypothesis of positive allometry in distal parts of wing and longer wings in female individuals in structurally open habitats (savanna and Caatinga vegetation) compared with those in closed habitats (forests). This reinforces the need for studies of phenotypic variation and plasticity in a microevolutionary fashion and not a priori generalizing to the entire lineage.
